strengths: Novel and principled theoretical perspective: reinterpreting Shampoo's Kronecker-factored second-moment estimation as KL-divergence-based covariance estimation rather than the commonly-used Frobenius-norm view, which naturally respects the SPD constraint on the preconditioner.

Clean, rigorous derivations (Claims 1–3 with full proofs in the appendix) that clearly show Shampoo is optimal only for a restricted one-sided preconditioner and motivate a jointly-optimal two-sided estimator.

The resulting algorithm (KL-Shampoo) is practically appealing: it removes the need for Adam-based step-size grafting, thereby reducing memory overhead, and is compatible with efficient QR-based updates (avoiding costly eigendecompositions), extending naturally to tensor-valued weights (e.g., MoE layers).

Reasonably broad empirical validation across four different architectures (NanoGPT, RWKV7, Llama, NanoMoE) and datasets, with fairly extensive hyperparameter search (120 runs per method) showing consistent improvements over Shampoo (with/without grafting) and matching or exceeding SOAP's efficiency.
weaknesses: The authors themselves repeatedly label the results as 'preliminary,' and the paper is very short (6 pages of main text), suggesting the work is not yet a complete, mature submission for a top-tier venue.

Experimental scale is limited: all models are small (123M–227M parameters) trained on modest token budgets (1B–2.5B tokens); no evidence is given that the approach scales to larger, more realistic pretraining settings.

No error bars, multiple seeds, or variance reporting are shown in the loss curves, making it hard to assess whether the reported improvements over SOAP/Shampoo are statistically meaningful given the known noisiness of optimizer comparisons.

The 'idealized' KL-Shampoo update (Eq. 4) resolves the circular dependency between S_a* and S_b* via a heuristic moving-average scheme; the paper claims this can be justified via a proximal-gradient framework but does not actually present this justification or any convergence analysis in the paper.

No ablation studies isolating which component (joint two-sided estimation, QR-based eigenvalue update, or removal of grafting) drives the empirical gains, making it difficult to attribute the source of improvement.

Missing comparisons to other recent structured/adaptive optimizers beyond Shampoo variants and SOAP (e.g., Muon, PSGD, or other recently proposed Kronecker-based methods cited in the related work), and no direct comparison to plain Adam as a baseline.
No quantitative memory/compute savings table is provided to substantiate the claimed efficiency benefits of removing Adam grafting; efficiency claims rest only on wall-clock training curves.
Only pretraining test loss is reported; no downstream task evaluation is included to assess whether the loss improvements translate into practically meaningful gains.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely different theoretical lens (KL divergence / covariance-estimation view) for analyzing Shampoo's structured second-moment estimation, which naturally respects the SPD constraint that the Frobenius-norm analyses used by prior work (Morwani et al., Eschenhagen et al., Xie et al.) do not.

Provides clean, complete closed-form derivations (Claims 1-3) with full proofs in the appendix, giving a principled explanation for why Shampoo's one-sided estimation is suboptimal relative to a jointly-optimized two-sided estimator.

The resulting algorithm (KL-Shampoo with QR-based eigenbasis/eigenvalue updates) is a practical, implementable variant that removes the need for Adam-based step-size grafting, which is an appealing efficiency/memory benefit if it holds up.

Experiments span four architecturally diverse models (including an MoE model with genuinely tensor-valued weights), showing the method generalizes beyond the matrix-weight case emphasized in prior analyses.
Fairly extensive hyperparameter search (120 runs per method) for each baseline suggests an attempt at fair comparison rather than cherry-picked settings.
weaknesses: The paper repeatedly self-describes its results as 'preliminary' (abstract, introduction, conclusion), which is a direct admission that the empirical validation is not yet mature enough to support the claimed contributions at a top-tier venue standard.

All experiments are on small-to-medium models (123M-227M parameters) trained on relatively small token budgets (1-2.5B tokens); there is no scaling study or evidence that the claimed advantages persist at larger, more realistic LLM pretraining scales, which is critical for credibility of optimizer papers.

No variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported for the final comparison curves (Figs. 1-2), despite the random search over 120 runs; it is unclear whether the reported curves are single best runs or averages, undermining confidence that the observed gains are statistically robust.
No wall-clock or memory quantification table is given despite the central claim that KL-Shampoo saves memory by removing Adam grafting; only qualitative statements are made.

No ablation isolating the individual contributions of the proposed components (joint two-sided estimation vs. the moving-average eigenvalue scheme vs. QR-based eigenbasis updates), making it hard to know which design choice drives the empirical improvement.

The practical algorithm relies on several heuristic approximations (single-sample E[gg^T] approximation, outdated eigenbasis reuse, moving-average fixed point justified only briefly via a 'proximal-gradient framework' without detailed derivation in the main text), reducing the rigor gap between the clean theory and the actual deployed method.

The closed-form two-sided estimator (Eq. 3) is acknowledged to have been proposed before (Lin et al. 2019/2024) and a closely related heuristic already explored by Vyas et al. (2025b, SOAP+Muon), yet no direct empirical comparison to that closely related concurrent work is provided, limiting the novelty argument.
No theoretical convergence analysis or guarantees are provided for the proposed estimator or algorithm, despite the optimization-theoretic framing.

The paper is short (6 pages main text) with limited experimental depth/ablations typical of a mature full submission, and overall feels more like an early-stage workshop contribution than a complete, rigorously validated paper.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel theoretical lens (KL divergence between Gaussians) for interpreting Shampoo's Kronecker-factored second-moment estimation, in contrast to prior Frobenius-norm-based analyses, and shows this view naturally respects the SPD constraint required for a valid descent direction.

The KL perspective yields a concrete, previously unrecognized limitation of Shampoo (it does not jointly minimize KL over both Kronecker factors), which directly motivates a principled new estimation rule (Claims 2 and 3) rather than an ad hoc heuristic.
The approach generalizes beyond the matrix case and is demonstrated on tensor-valued weights (NanoMoE), which is a plus relative to several prior Frobenius-based analyses that focus only on matrices.

A practically efficient implementation is developed (QR-based eigenvalue/eigenbasis estimation) that avoids the costly eigendecomposition and matrix inversions implied by the idealized KL-Shampoo update, making the method competitive in wall-clock time with SOAP.

Empirical results span four different architectures (GPT-style, RWKV7, Llama, MoE) and show KL-Shampoo removes the need for Adam-based step-size grafting while matching or exceeding SOAP's efficiency and outperforming Shampoo, with a reasonably extensive hyperparameter search (120 runs per method).
All theoretical claims are accompanied by clear, self-contained proofs in the appendix, aiding reproducibility of the derivations.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly frames its results as 'preliminary,' and indeed the empirical evaluation is limited to small models (123M-227M parameters) and short training budgets (1-2.5B tokens), which is modest for validating an optimizer intended for large-scale pretraining; no evidence is given that the benefits persist at larger scale.

No error bars, variance across seeds, or statistical significance analysis accompany the loss curves in Figures 1-2, despite using single best/selected runs from a 120-run search; it is unclear how robust the reported gains are to run-to-run variability.

There is a theory-practice gap: the idealized KL-Shampoo (Claim 2) is computationally infeasible and the deployed QR-based method (Claim 3, Fig. 3) is a further heuristic approximation (outdated eigenbasis, moving-average eigenvalue estimate) whose optimality or convergence properties relative to the original KL objective are not established; the justification via a 'proximal-gradient framework' is asserted but not shown in the main text.

No ablation studies isolating the individual contributions of the two main innovations (joint two-sided KL estimation vs. the QR/eigenvalue-estimation efficiency trick), making it hard to attribute the empirical gains to either component specifically.

The comparison to the closely related heuristic in Vyas et al. (2025b), which proposes a similar closed-form whitening-based update, is only discussed qualitatively; no direct empirical comparison is provided despite its clear relevance.
No wall-clock/memory accounting details (e.g., exact peak memory savings from removing Adam states) are quantified numerically, despite memory reduction being a central motivating claim of the paper.
Evaluation is restricted to language modeling pretraining; no experiments on other domains (vision, fine-tuning, RL) are included to support claims of general applicability.
No code release or explicit reproducibility artifacts are mentioned, which is a concern given the method's implementation complexity (QR updates, moving-average eigenvalues, damping).

strengths: Introduces a novel and principled KL-divergence perspective on Shampoo/SOAP preconditioner estimation, contrasting with prior Frobenius-norm-based analyses, and grounds this in information geometry / quasi-Newton connections.

Rigorous theoretical development: multiple formal claims (one-sided vs. two-sided Kronecker estimation, eigenvalue correction under stale eigenbasis, RMSProp-in-eigenbasis as augmented eigenvalue estimation) with complete proofs in the appendix.
Reveals a concrete and previously unrecognized limitation of Shampoo/SOAP's one-sided Kronecker estimator relative to the KL-optimal two-sided solution, which directly motivates the proposed method.
Provides an efficient practical implementation (QR-based, EMA on eigenvalues with stale eigenbasis) that matches SOAP's per-iteration runtime while avoiding Adam's memory overhead in KL-Shampoo.
Thorough empirical study across four different LM architectures (including a 3D-tensor MoE model), with a careful two-stage random hyperparameter search (150 runs) for fair comparisons.

Includes ablations comparing KL divergence against Frobenius-norm and von Neumann divergence variants (F-Shampoo, VN-Shampoo), reimplemented consistently to reduce implementation bias, providing evidence that the KL choice is empirically superior.
Interesting practical finding that KL-Shampoo removes reliance on Adam step-size grafting, simplifying the optimizer and reducing memory.
weaknesses: All experiments are on relatively small models (123M-227M parameters) trained on small token budgets (1-2.5B tokens); it is unclear whether the observed advantages persist at larger scale or longer training, which is important given Shampoo/SOAP's primary use case in large-scale pretraining.

The counterintuitive result that KL-Shampoo outperforms KL-SOAP (i.e., adding Adam in the eigenbasis hurts performance) is reported but not deeply analyzed or theoretically explained, leaving a central empirical finding under-motivated.

No comparison to other recent structured/adaptive optimizers mentioned in the introduction (e.g., Muon, ASGO) despite these being discussed as related work; the empirical comparison set is essentially limited to Shampoo/SOAP variants.

Results are based on random hyperparameter search with best runs plotted; it is unclear whether variance across seeds/runs is reported, making it hard to assess statistical robustness of the reported gains.

The idealized two-sided KL-Shampoo update requires correlated, generally infeasible joint optimization (Claim 2), and the practical EMA/stale-eigenbasis approximation used in practice departs from the theoretical optimum, so the paper's practical guarantees rest more on empirical tuning than the theory strictly established.

The core mathematical result connecting two-sided Kronecker KL-minimization to matrix-Gaussian MLE is already known in prior literature (acknowledged citations to Dutilleul 1999, Lin et al. 2019/2024), somewhat limiting the novelty of the central theoretical contribution beyond re-deriving and operationalizing it for Shampoo/SOAP.

strengths: Provides a novel and coherent theoretical framing of Shampoo/SOAP's structured second-moment estimation as KL-divergence-based covariance estimation, with formal proofs (Claims 1-7) that cleanly identify a real limitation: Shampoo/SOAP's Kronecker estimators solve a one-sided rather than two-sided KL problem.

The KL perspective naturally extends to tensor-valued weights, and the paper also contrasts KL with Frobenius-norm and von Neumann divergence formulations, giving a fairly complete picture of why KL is a more natural choice (SPD-respecting, connects to BFGS/DFP literature).

Practical engineering contribution: replacing costly eigendecomposition with QR + EMA-based eigenvalue correction, enabling KL-Shampoo to match SOAP's per-iteration runtime while removing Adam's memory overhead (Table 1) and step-size grafting requirement.

Reasonably thorough empirical protocol: four distinct architectures (including a MoE model with genuine 3D tensor weights), two-stage random search with 150 runs per method per model, and several targeted ablations (Figs. 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10) isolating the effect of two-sided estimation, EMA eigenvalue correction, and divergence choice.
weaknesses: Novelty is diminished by very closely related concurrent/prior work explicitly acknowledged in the paper: Vyas et al. (2025b) propose essentially the same two-sided whitening condition motivated heuristically, and Lin et al. (2019, 2024) already treat this as a known theoretical example in the exponential-family/natural-gradient literature; the paper's main technical contribution is largely reframing and operationalizing these known ideas via KL rather than introducing a fundamentally new estimator.

All experiments are on small-scale language models (123M-227M parameters) trained on 1-2.5B tokens; there is no evidence the reported advantages persist at larger model/data scale, which is the regime where Shampoo-family optimizers are typically most relevant and where prior competition results (AlgoPerf) were obtained.

No variance/seed analysis is reported — results are presented as single best-of-random-search curves (or apparently single runs) without error bars or repeated seeds, making it hard to assess whether the reported gains (often visually small, e.g., NanoMoE in Fig. 1) are statistically meaningful versus noise from hyperparameter search variance.

The gap between 'idealized' KL-Shampoo (which requires unattainable joint fixed-point solving of Eq. 4) and the practical EMA-based implementation is justified only via a proximal-gradient heuristic (Claim 3) with a block-diagonal approximation of the Fisher-Rao metric; no convergence guarantee or bound on the approximation error is provided for the practical algorithm actually used in experiments.

Baselines and 'fair comparison' claims rely partly on the authors' own re-implementations of Shampoo variants (F-Shampoo, VN-Shampoo) rather than established/tuned reference implementations, raising some risk of implementation bias despite the stated intent to mitigate it.
No code release or explicit reproducibility artifacts are mentioned, and hyperparameter search ranges/final settings are not fully specified in the main text, limiting reproducibility.

The paper is entirely restricted to language-model pretraining; no evaluation on other domains (vision, fine-tuning, downstream tasks) or on wall-clock benefits at larger scale/distributed settings where Shampoo-style methods' overhead (e.g., all-reduce of eigenbases) is more consequential.

strengths: Provides a novel and unifying theoretical framework (KL/log-determinant divergence for covariance estimation) that cleanly interprets Shampoo's and SOAP's preconditioner estimation rules as special cases (one-sided vs two-sided KL minimization), and extends naturally to tensor-valued weights where SVD-based Frobenius interpretations do not apply.

Rigorous derivations (Claims 1-7 with full proofs in the appendix) connecting Shampoo/SOAP to KL minimization, and additionally situating Frobenius-norm and von-Neumann-divergence variants within a common Bregman-divergence framework, clarifying exactly how KL-Shampoo differs from prior 'two-sided'/trace-scaling proposals.

Strong practical contribution: an efficient QR-based implementation with an EMA eigenvalue-correction scheme that avoids costly eigendecomposition/matrix inversion, achieves SOAP-level per-iteration runtime, and removes the need for Adam-based step-size grafting, thereby saving the associated memory overhead (clearly quantified in Table 1).

Extensive and fairly designed empirical evaluation: 4 diverse architectures (GPT, RWKV7, Llama, MoE with 3D tensors) across different datasets, large hyperparameter searches (150 runs/method, two-stage refinement), self-reimplemented baselines to reduce implementation bias, and multiple targeted ablations (Figs. 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10) isolating the effect of two-sided estimation, EMA eigenvalue correction, and divergence choice (KL vs Frobenius vs VN).

Consistent and somewhat surprising empirical result that KL-Shampoo (without Adam) outperforms KL-SOAP, SOAP, and Shampoo across all tested settings, which is a meaningful and actionable finding for practitioners concerned with memory efficiency.
weaknesses: All experiments are conducted on relatively small models (123M-227M parameters) and modest token budgets (1-2.5B tokens); it is unclear whether the benefits of KL-Shampoo persist at the larger scales where Shampoo/SOAP are typically deployed in practice (e.g., billion-parameter LLM pretraining), which limits the significance of the claimed improvements.

Results are reported as single best/selected curves from a 150-run random search without variance, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed repetition at the chosen best hyperparameters; given the sensitivity of adaptive optimizers to hyperparameters, it is hard to assess statistical significance of the reported gaps (e.g., in Fig. 1 and Fig. 5).

The 'idealized' KL-Shampoo update (Claim 2/Eq. 4) is not directly achievable due to the correlated S_a/S_b dependency, and the practical EMA scheme (Eq. 5, Claim 3) relies on a block-diagonal approximation of the Fisher-Rao metric as the proximal weight matrix; the gap between the idealized theoretical justification and the practical heuristic (block-diagonal truncation, use of outdated eigenbasis) is not empirically quantified beyond aggregate loss curves.

The paper does not include evaluations beyond language modeling (e.g., vision transformers, other domains) despite Shampoo/SOAP's broad applicability, nor downstream/fine-tuning task evaluation, limiting generality claims.

Some ablations (Figs. 7, 9) show that naive 'idealized' F-Shampoo/VN-Shampoo perform poorly and only become competitive after borrowing KL-Shampoo's EMA/QR machinery; this raises the question of how much of the empirical improvement is attributable to the KL divergence itself versus the shared engineering tricks (EMA eigenvalue correction, QR schedule) applied uniformly across variants.
